1.1: 1.1 Preface. Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, produced three volumes according to the number of his names. The first of these is Mishle, which the Greeks and Latins call Proverbs, because in it, under comparative likeness, he shows figures of words and images of the truth, but reserved the truth itself to be understood by the ingenuity of the readers. The second book he called Coheleth, which is called in Greek and in Latin Concionator (the Preacher), because its addresses are directed not only spiritually to one person, as in Proverbs, but to all generally, teaching that all things we see in the world are vain and brief, and for that reason by no means to be sought. The third book he entitled Shir Hashirim, which is turned into the Latin tongue as Song of Songs, where through a wedding song he sings mystically of the union of Christ and the Church. It is called the Song of Songs because it is preferred to all songs, just as in the law certain things are called holy, above which are greater, the holy of holies. In these three books he composed the disciplines of three kinds, by which knowledge of things is reached: first ethics, that is, moral; after this physics, which comprehends the quality of nature; finally theoretics, that is, contemplative. For in Proverbs, teaching moral matters, through a certain common usage of speech he put forth a loftier understanding, and in concise words and brief sentences he fits together the keeping of the commandments and the instruction of heavenly teaching. Proverbs are those which explain one thing under other words, which are understood otherwise than as they are said; they have more in the force of their meanings than in the sound of their words; the Greeks call them [a Greek term omitted]. Ecclesiastes, examining the natures of things, finds all things in the world to be vain and perishing, and, having observed the fragility of all things, warned men to renounce the world. In the Song of Songs, rising above visible things and contemplating those that are heavenly or divine, under the appearance of bridegroom and bride he declares the unity of Christ and the Church, and, stirring the soul to the love of heavenly things, summons it to come to fellowship with God. But one must not think what is handed down by our hearers, that among the Hebrews this was the practice, that they would permit no one to read this book unless a man already of perfect knowledge and of strengthened faith in skill, lest the knowledge instruct slippery minds less than the text turn them to bodily desires. Solomon, that is, peaceable, because in his reign there was peace, by which the future peace of the Church was prefigured; Jedidiah, that is, beloved, and it signifies him of whom it is said: You are beautiful in form above the sons of men; therefore God has blessed you forever (Psalm 44). Ecclesiastes, that is, preacher, and it signifies him who was to speak reasonably and to gather the Church. According to the number of his names, he made three books: Proverbs, in which he teaches little ones, not so much in age as in wisdom, about calm conduct in the world, namely how they may lawfully use temporal things; Ecclesiastes, in which he instructs men of more advanced age to despise perishable things; the Song of Songs, namely this work, in which he teaches the perfected man about the love of God alone, that he may rest between the arms of the bridegroom. Hence it is also called the Song of Songs, excelling all other songs in its dignity. For through those vices are avoided and the enemy guarded against; through these we are enriched with virtues and joined to the Lord. In a similar order the philosophers also set out their teachings: first they teach ethics, afterward physics, and one whom they see to have advanced in these they lead on up to theoretics. The subject matter: the bridegroom and the bride, that is, the head and the Church. And the manner: with what desire the members cling to the head and strive to please him, and what gifts they receive from him either in the present or look for in the future, and with what affection the bridegroom loves the Church, praising her, and admonishing, and strengthening her. The end is the love of God. In this work I seem to myself to find four persons: the bridegroom and his companions, the bride and the maidens with her. Some things are said by the bridegroom, some by the bride; a number by the young women, certain ones by the companions of the bridegroom. It is fitting indeed that at the beginning there be a multitude of maidens with the bride, a crowd of young men with the bridegroom. By the bridegroom understand Christ; by the bride the Church without spot or wrinkle. By the friends of the bridegroom understand the angels, and those who have attained to the perfect man. The maidens are the crowds of beginning brides, who have obtained salvation in a certain measure. From this book the Gentiles claimed for themselves the wedding song, and a song of this kind was adopted. If you wish to ascend to the Song of Songs, it is necessary to go out of Egypt, so that after the crossing of the Red Sea, with the enemies drowned, you may first be able to sing the song: Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously, etc. (Exodus 15). But since you are still far from the Song of Songs, travel spiritually through the land of the desert, and then, set at the bank of the Jordan, sing the second song: Hear, O heavens, the things I speak, etc. (Deuteronomy 31). And when you have passed over all, ascend to higher things, so that as a soul adorned with the bridegroom you may sing this Song of Songs also. It is to be noted that the bride always desires to stay in the house, or in the bed, or in some inner place with the bridegroom, which suits women. He, as is the way of males, summons his beloved to the outer parts of the vineyards, or to works of this kind, because the Church, if it could be, desires to raise offspring for the Lord in the tranquility of peace. But he in the present exercises her with frequent persecutions, that she may come the purer to eternal things, lest, if prosperity befall her, delighted by sojourning in the present age or exile, she sigh less for the heavenly homeland. The Synagogue is a congregation, which is said also of stones; the Church is a convocation, which is said of rational beings. But each portion of the just, in the same faith and love of Christ at different times, the one by awaiting him who was to come, the other by receiving him who is present, has been made a sharer. God, the founder of the universe, created all the motions of the soul for good, but through our use it often happens that things which are good by nature, while we abuse them badly, lead us to sin. One of the motions of the soul is love, which we use well if we love wisdom and truth, but badly if we love flesh or blood. You, therefore, as a spiritual person, hear spiritually the loving words of the song being sung, and learn to transfer the motion of your soul and the fire of natural love to better things. Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. The voice of those who precede the coming of Christ, who pray to the father of the bridegroom, that is, of Christ. In the midst of their prayers she is heard, and seeing the bridegroom she speaks to him: Let him touch me with the sweetness of his presence, which I have heard oftentimes promised by the prophets, and, bringing as it were a kiss, let him also receive the touch of my mouth; that is, let him hear me as I ask about the way of salvation, and, making both one, let him bring the kiss of peace. To kiss is put for to be reconciled, after the likeness of those who withdrew from their lords on account of discord, but, returning, kiss one another and are perfectly reconciled; so the Synagogue, the human race removed from God by sin, wishes to be reconciled through the incarnation of the Son. As many commandments as she learns from his preaching, so many kisses of his mouth she receives, as it were. She speaks in the manner of a lover, who in the fervor of love cannot keep the order of speaking. For as in a kiss two different bodies are joined, so in the incarnation of the Son two substances, of divinity and humanity, utterly different, are united in an inseparable union. For your breasts are better. She names the breasts of the bridegroom Christ, which is a womanly thing, to show from the very beginning of the song that she speaks figuratively. Therefore I desire the kiss, which is also my redemption, because your instructions, which are the milk and nourishment of children, are better than other teachings, which do not cherish but kill the simple, as wine kills little ones. By the fragrance of ointments the reputation of virtues is usually signified.
1.2: 1.2 Your name is oil poured out. Therefore I also desire the kiss, because your name is oil, etc. The bridegroom came from the Father to the bride anointed, that he might also anoint the bride. Christ is from chrisma, that is, anointed from anointing; which name is poured out through the grace of the Holy Spirit in baptism upon all the faithful. I cannot yet embrace you yourself; in the meantime your name, out of longing for you, will spend the night with me. The name of Jesus came into the world, and at once is preached. Oil poured out, that is, over the whole earth the name of Christ is preached; now the name of Moses is heard among the Gentiles, which before was confined only in the narrow bounds of Judea. Therefore the maidens have loved you. Saying this, she catches sight of the maidens, who were not present while she was speaking before, but in the midst of the prayers the chorus of maidens enters and is praised in the words of the bride. All the Churches, which make up the one catholic Church, are the maidens: not aged by guilt but new by grace, not barren with old age but, by the age of the mind, suited for spiritual fruitfulness. And because with the oil of your grace you have emptied out all the sorrows of crimes, Therefore the maidens, etc.
1.3: 1.3 Draw me after you. The maidens answer: Draw me after you. The bride does not follow behind the back, but, joined to the bridegroom's side, her handmaids go in after her. Draw me after you. Up to this point is the voice of those awaiting the incarnation of the Savior and commending his gifts; from here follows the voice of those who came to the faith after the time of the incarnation. The former asked that he come and offer a kiss; the latter do not so demand that he descend to them, but desire rather to follow him themselves to the heavens; and because she sees this cannot be done by herself, she implores the guidance of him to whom she desires to come. Unto the fragrance of your ointments. In the consideration of the miracles. The king has brought me in, etc. The bride, having entered the inner chamber of the bridegroom, returns to the young women and announces to them: He has brought me in. Or, through hope he has led me into eternal blessedness; in the plural, for the fullness of every kind of good, as if I had already tasted beforehand the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom; the things prepared for me in heaven I have come to know by his own revealing; and soon, turned to him who reveals this to her, she gives thanks for the benefits. There are four things in a house: the gate, the ascent, the dining hall, the bedchamber. By the gate we understand faith; by the ascent, hope; by the dining hall, charity; by the bedchamber, blessedness itself. We will exult and rejoice. As if she said: We do not exalt ourselves over the gifts received, but exalt you, mindful in all things with what great kindness you deigned to soften the austerity of the law by the grace of the gospel faith; therefore we will exult not in ourselves but in you, because all the upright love you, and have learned that you are to be loved above all things. Again the bride has entered the inner chamber, and the maidens, while they await her coming, sing joyfully together for the perfection of the bride. Mindful of your breasts. And the upright love: this is referred to the commendation of the bride. Mindful of your breasts, etc. She who is greater already enjoys the milk of your breasts. We too do not indeed love, but we shall love. Then they speak to the bridegroom: The upright love you. The upright: all who are upright of heart love you above all things, and they are not upright who put anything before your love, from whom alone they have whatever good they have. The upright love. In vain do they believe they love the Creator who despise his admonitions. The truly just violate God neither in deed, nor in thought, nor in word.
1.4: 1.4 I am black. After the Church was led into the cellars, that is, through knowledge and through hope of the good things to come, after she learned to love him with an upright heart and to rejoice in his grace, it remains to show that for love of him and for the acquisition of the goods she has tasted she undergoes the struggle, and what affliction she bears. I am black. As if she said: You promise that you will go with me, and the tribulation which I suffer can deter you; but let neither affliction nor ill repute deter you, because these will confer the beauty of the virtues, and after love there remains patience for the proof of love. I am black. Again the bride answers the maidens, and the matter treated is manifest temptation. I am black. I appear indeed contemptible in the eyes of the persecutors, but before God I shine glorious by the confession of the truth. Like the tents of Kedar. Here like is put not for the truth but for the estimation of the foolish, who think her the dwelling of vices or of demons; like the skins of Solomon is put here for the truth. Kedar was a son of Ishmael, whose hand was against all, and the hand of all against him, having no place among men, but dwelling always in tents, because of wickedness and wrath. So the just also are believed, on account of their merits, to be driven out and afflicted, and are judged as enemies of all; hence it is said: You shall be hated by all men for my name's sake (Matthew 10). Like the feet. The Church, mortifying carnal desires in herself and adorned with virtues, becomes a worthy dwelling for the true Peaceable One. Therefore the flesh of the Lord's humanity is called a skin, because as a tent is stretched over someone lest he be scorched by the sun, so the flesh of Christ stretched on the cross was for us a shading from vices.
1.5: 1.5 The sun has discolored me. It belongs to the sun to burn and to illuminate; so the true sun outwardly burns his own with persecutions, and by giving strength to resist, enlightens them. The sons of my mother. And, as if to the objection of the weak who doubt, she answers: She shows whence she bore the first fury of the persecutors, which appears the more grievous in that it comes from fellow-sufferers. The sons, that is, the apostles, destroyed our sect. Paul, persecutor of the Church, was a son of her mother according to the flesh and upbringing; and doing penance, turned to the signs of the sister, he preached the faith which he formerly destroyed. They have made me. There was one vineyard of Christ in Jerusalem, namely the primitive Church, which was established on the day of Pentecost by the coming of the Holy Spirit, and of which the apostles were at that time the keepers; but when persecution arose they were scattered in the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles, and so it happened that there were many vineyards, that is, in many places. And while the Jewish persecutors wished to disturb the Church, they spread the seedbed of the word more widely, unwilling, and by persecuting one, caused many to be established. Having then said that she was afflicted by the parricidal hatred of the Synagogue, she soon adds how much she has gained by this affliction, adding in the person of those to whom the care of preaching was committed: They have made me keeper in the vineyards. GREGORY. Our vineyards are our actions, which we cultivate by the practice of daily labor. But set as keepers in the vineyards, we do not keep our own vineyard, because while we are entangled in external actions, we neglect the ministry of our own action. While I was keeping many vineyards, in order to gain others, in some I sustained losses. The bitterness of the persecution by the sons of the Synagogue made me not keep my own vineyard, because, the gospel teaching having been abandoned, they were forcing me to the differences of legal observances.
1.6: 1.6 Show me, etc. The voice of the Church beginning from the Gentiles to the bride, because many false prophets go out into the world saying: Behold, here is Christ, behold, there; she begs that she may be able to discern in whose profession and work he can be found. Show me my shepherd, whom my whole soul loves, and in whom he has rest and pastures, lest, disturbed by the heat of temptations, I begin to seek him through the gatherings of companions, that is, of heretics. Or it is in the voice of the preachers to the bridegroom, that they may be able to discern to whom they ought to minister the words of life. Then she beholds the bridegroom, who, once beheld, departed. And this he does frequently in the whole song, which she has proved by experience in herself: the bridegroom, often held, often slips away, until he is truly held. At noon, etc. That is, in the splendor of your majesty, which befits the perfect, not at morning or evening. Or, at noon, that is, in the burning of tribulations, which the devil sends, grieving that the world is being snatched from him. The quality of things is usually noted from the time. Abraham received the angels at noon. Joseph feasts with his brothers at noon. Of your companions. Heretics are called companions, because they carry about the mysteries of his name and confession.
1.7: 1.7 If you do not know. Because the bride, while seeking the aid of God's presence in tribulations, had added, in the person of the weak, Lest I begin to wander, the bridegroom, being implored, at once rebukes that same trembling with kindly reproach, according to the Gospel saying, O you of little faith (Matthew 14), as if he said: You fear being destroyed by me in tribulation, and in the heat you complain that you have been blackened; but I have determined by tribulations to make you more beautiful. But if perhaps you do not know this, nor remember that no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully, go out from my company. GREGORY, Moralia, book 16, chapter 21. She knows herself when, placed in mind among sinners, she remembers that she was made in the image of her Author and walks according to the order of the likeness received; but if she does not know it, she goes out from the secret of the heart into outward desires, and, led to the broad way, follows the examples of the peoples. The Lord, rebuking the fearful Church, reminds her of the grace given her against the snares of enemies. Your kids. Because they are trained not according to the rule of my commandments, but according to your errors. Beside, in the footsteps of the shepherds you will be last, not among the sheep but the kids. Or beside, that is, that you may be like the true shepherds, because hypocrites seem to follow good men.
1.8: 1.8 To the cavalry. As I freed the former people from Egyptian slavery, so I will free you from the hands of the persecutors, crushing Pharaoh, if you recognize yourself as my bride, freeing you from the slavery of the devil in the font of baptism reddened by the passion, the author of sin being drowned there. To my cavalry. Because the Lord does not wish the Church to be ignorant of herself, but diligently to attend to what gifts she has received and what she must suffer, after the threat he consequently coaxes her, as if he said: If you wish to understand how you ought to know yourself, understand to whom I have compared you, and then you will know yourself to be such through my benefits conferred on you, so that you ought not to be troubled. To the cavalry. The horseman is the bridegroom, as the prophet says: And his salvation is a riding (Habakkuk 3). As much then as my cavalry differs from the horses of Pharaoh, so much better are you than all other daughters. As that people was terrified by the chariots of Pharaoh coming upon them, but was saved by heavenly protection, and, the enemies drowned through the waters, was brought into the promised land, so the wave of death, which will meet all mortals, snatches the wicked to destruction and opens to the pious the way to salvation, and all the rest, which was fulfilled there bodily, is fulfilled here spiritually. He kindly rebukes the one who doubts, and lest she despair he strengthens her manfully in the faithful love that follows, where he compares her to Pharaoh's chariots. In the chariots of Pharaoh. That is, in the time of the chariots. And note the pride: Pharaoh is interpreted as crushing or scattering. Nor is it necessary that you begin to wander, since you have me as consoler, and prelates on whom you may lean, through whom you may stand firm.
1.9: 1.9 Fair. Since it has been shown how the Lord protects the Church amid adversities, it remains to be shown how much love of the Lord himself the Church keeps amid adversities. Whence follows, Fair are your cheeks. I have adorned you with such virtue of saving modesty that no teaching or suggestion of perverse teachers may corrupt the chastity of the faith promised to me, from whom you feared being led into error. The beauty of a woman is said to be chiefly in the cheeks. Allegorically. In the cheeks is noted the sign of modesty, as in preachers the habit of living rightly. The Church, though widowed by the death of her Spouse, yet is held by such memory of him that she can in no way receive the fellowship of strangers: and groans for her own and others' sins. In the neck, the teachers, in the necklaces their works: because what they teach by word, they do. What is the grace of keeping this sobriety, he shows by adding. Your neck as necklaces. For through the neck we pass food into the body to be refreshed, and we bring forth words with which we declare the secrets of the heart to neighbors, that is, teachers who both instruct by words, and pour the food of salvation into the members committed to them. Who are compared to necklaces, who are fair in morals, and enclose the breasts of virgins with words and examples, lest the adulterer put in his hand.
1.10: 1.10 Little chains. Another translation. We will make you likenesses of gold, inlaid with silver, until the king is at his repose. That is, gold, that is, my face you cannot see in the present life, but the likeness of heavenly brightness, through the illumination of the Scriptures, you will see through a glass in a riddle, until to all appears what now is hid in the Godhead. Little chains. The Bridegroom beautifully describes her beauty: after this he becomes her Bridegroom in repose. Meanwhile, he sleeping, his companions, that is the angels, console her; we have not gold, but we will cause a likeness of gold to be made for you, until he arise with marks of silver. Little chains. Whatever good institutions, like ornaments of the ears. In the little chains the holy Scripture, which shines within with the gold of spiritual senses, and glitters without with the silver of heavenly speech; through the edification of teachers there is the guarding of sobriety, and through the meditation of the divine Scripture. Shining within and without with the gold of divine wisdom and the silver of divine speech. We will make. I and my workmen, whom I have appointed in great number to distribute the seeds of the word.
1.11: 1.11 While the king was. The Church, having received such gifts and promises from her founder, makes manifest with what devotion of works she has received them, saying: While the king was, that is, when the Son of God appeared in the flesh, the Church through the very mystery of the incarnation grew into the fervor of heavenly virtues. Or, when he was in the humiliation of the cross the human race redeemed through the cross, the exercise of good works scattered the odor of sweetness. Christ the king resting in the beatitude of heavenly secrecy, the virtue of the saints in the Church ministers to us great grace of sweetness, who the less they see him whom they seek, the more ardently they burn with desire. Or, while he was with the Father, the nard, that is the love with which he first loved us, gave odor, because through love for our sake he took flesh. A wonderful order of words. The king reclining my nard gave its odor, while for the excess of charity with which he loved us, he was made the son of a woman. Nard, which is said to drive away swellings, put cold to flight and bring heat; to which the Lord's humanity is likened, who by taking flesh humbled himself, and by humbling himself took away every swelling of pride, removed the cold of unbelief, and brought the fervor of charity. This herb also, the more it is crushed, the greater odor it renders, so Christ.
1.12: 1.12 A bundle. The death of my beloved, which he underwent for my salvation, will always abide in my memory. Likewise he is compared to a bundle of myrrh, since for our sake he endured the injuries of the cross. Myrrh is a tree of Arabia, five cubits high, like the spike which they call acanthus, whose drop is green and bitter, whence it took the name myrrh. Its drop flowing of itself is more precious, cheaper when drawn out by a wound of the bark, and is wholesome for healing infirmities: whence he also received myrrhed wine from the soldiers. My breasts. The breasts of the chaste are not broken; but those of harlots are wrinkled with slack skin. Whence Ezekiel: In Egypt your breasts were broken, Ezekiel 23.
1.13: 1.13 My beloved is a cluster of cypress. A cluster of cypress when he rose: In the vineyards of Engaddi, when he distributes spiritual gifts to the faithful. The balsam trees that grow in Engaddi, because they are cultivated in the manner of vineyards, he calls vineyards. The Bridegroom Christ is therefore in the vineyards of Engaddi, because coming in the flesh full of the Holy Spirit, he bestows on believers the gifts of the same Holy Spirit through the anointing of chrism, in whose making oil and balsam are mixed. Engaddi, fountain of the kid, on account of the gifts which after the resurrection he bestowed in baptism on his partakers. Engaddi, that is the eye of my temptation, and the life of man upon earth is a temptation. Because the glory of the resurrection soon followed the death of the Mediator, it is rightly added, A cluster, who was a bundle of myrrh in the bitterness of the passion, in the sweetness of the resurrection was a cluster of cypress. For myrrh saddens, wine gladdens.
1.14: 1.14 Behold you are fair. Hitherto the Church, who has received pledges of love from the Bridegroom, testifies, to whom he soon answers as a reward: Behold you are fair; as if, because you love me, you shall be made fair. My love. Another translation: My nearest; that is, in that you are nearest you are beautiful, and after you begin to be beautiful, you are fair without addition. Your eyes. Another praise of the beautiful bride, that we also may labor to become beautiful. Your eyes of doves, you look upon God simply because you seek nothing but him. He that sees a woman to lust after her, Matthew 5., has not the eyes of a dove; but he that has, beholds with chaste eyes, and understands the law and the Gospel spiritually. In whose form of a dove the Holy Spirit appeared. And therefore spiritual understanding, and all spiritual gifts are designated by the name of dove. The dove lacks gall, hurts not with the beak, builds nests in the clefts of rocks, nourishes strange young, abides by the streams, chooses the better grains, gives a moan for a song, flies in flocks, defends herself with wings, recovers sight. So the saints sitting by the streams of doctrine choose the better sentences, nourish for God men alien to Christ, if they find any good sentences in heretics they do not pervert them, lack unreasonable anger, in faith have refuge in the wounds of Christ, groan for sins.
1.15: 1.15 Behold you are fair, my beloved, and comely. The bride, hearing that she has merited by the love of the Bridegroom to be praised by the Bridegroom himself, returns the praise to the Bridegroom: not that she bestows on him by her heralding what he has not, but understanding his comeliness, by which she herself was made comely, she says: Behold you are fair, etc. Our bed is flourishing. Sometimes the Church rests as in a bed with the Bridegroom, in time of peace, namely, where she beholds the beauty of God more clearly, and begets from water and the Holy Spirit a progeny of the faithful fragrant with the flower of faith. Sometimes, temptation arising with the Bridegroom, she stands in the battle line. Or, the bed, the little faithful, who are rest to God and to their masters, by this at least, that they will not sin mortally, who flourish in the beginnings of good works, by which they give hope of fruit, that is of greater works. Wishing to lead a quiet life in the Bridegroom, she intimates of what sort the houses are in which she wishes to receive him. The peace of the Church flourishes with virtues and is multiplied by spiritual offspring.
1.16: 1.16 The beams of our houses are of cedar. The houses are the various Churches of the Gentiles through the world; The beams, which are wont to be made for the strength of the house, the preachers, by whose word and example the structure of the Church is held that it fall not. The ceilings, which are wont to be made for the beauty of the house, the simpler servants of Christ, who cling to the beams and are sustained, who adorn not by doctrine but by virtues. Cypress. It is called cypress in Greek, because its top is raised from roundness to a point: whence also it is called turben, that is high roundness, hence also its fruit is called cone: whence, Cone-bearing cypresses.
2.1: 2.1 I am the flower. Because labor suits the state of the present time more than rest: rightly she provokes the bride, delighted with leisure, to exercises of labor. As if he said: You indeed, wishing to render your beauty commendable to me, delight to flourish in the secrets of virtues in quiet: but know that I require another kind of beauty in the present, because I am the flower of virtues, from which every fruit of the field comes forth; because I desire my odor to be known to the whole world, which cannot be fulfilled unless, the quiet in which you delight being interrupted, you gird yourself for the office of preaching. And the lily of the valleys rather than of the mountains, because the brightness of my humanity, or the splendor of eternal light, or of the Godhead I reveal rather to the humble and those ready to suffer. As: Remember that I who could be born of a virgin, who am God, appeared humbly in the world, showed myself a companion to men, came humbly even to death. Therefore cease to seek the security of quiet, whence he adds, As the lily. As the field is adorned with flowers, so the world is adorned with my knowledge and faith.
2.2: 2.2 As the lily. Having praised himself, he praises the bride, thus: As the lily cannot be compared to the thorns among which it often springs: in the same way my nearest is above all the daughters a lily. As the lily. You seek rest and the praises of the bed: but know that you will be made whiter by the stings of tribulations, and the fruit of preaching is greater than of quiet. So my love. GREGORY. In the Church neither can the wicked be without the good, nor the good without the wicked: he was not good who could not bear the wicked. By the dogmas of adverse heresies her integrity is pricked as by thorns, that watching against her enemies she may be exercised, until eminent, like a lily, on the head of her Bridegroom, she is adorned with that very whiteness.
2.3: 2.3 As the apple tree, etc. The bride, praised and by the example of the Bridegroom admonished to suffer, exalts the Bridegroom with a return of praise, that among the works of the good he, singularly, stands out holy likewise, and promises to bear what she suffers, he presiding who is refreshment and restoration. As the apple tree. The odor of ointments, though it smells sweetly, is yet not sweet to eat. The apple, however, of best savor and odor, is such that it delights the palate with sweetness and soothes the spirit by its smell. Under the shadow. Therefore I set forth my beloved to all, because in the protection alone of his piety, whose desire I burned with, I see I have found refreshment from tribulations, and I feel the most sweet fruit of his gifts, with which I trust I shall be refreshed forever. She had desired, however, to breathe under the shadow of the author, when she complained that she was darkened by the sun of persecution, when imploring the help of God she cried: Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you lie down at noon; when not only weary with the tedium of pressures, but allured by the remembrance of his beauty and comeliness, she said: Our bed is flourishing; of which desire she shows herself made partaker, saying: Under the shadow. And it is to be noted that above she proclaimed the cedar beams and the cypress ceilings, yet she did not remember their protection as sufficient for her; but sought the tree of life alone, in whose shadow she might rest, and with whose fruit be refreshed, because the saints bring help by examples, doctrine, and intercession: yet to the Savior alone have we to say, But the children of men shall put their trust under the covert of your wings, Psalm 35. I sat and his fruit, etc. She does not say I sit, but I sat. Such are the advances of the Churches, that at the beginning one desires to sit in the shadow of virtues that his body may come to him from whom the shadow is born: therefore the nativity of Jesus also began from a shadow, and ends in truth. As it is said: The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you, Luke 1. So afterward the passage is made to better things. Sweet. Because in him the soul understands the cause of life, while it also perceives bodily.
2.4: 2.4 He brought me in. How great sweetness and how great power this refreshment has is shown when she adds, He brought me in. That is, by the hope of future glory he so gladdened that I now feel not the labors of the world. He brought me in. AMBROSE. As soon as my throat touched the sweetness of his grace, I feel myself so recreated in spirit and carried from the love of earthly things to the heavenly, as if, brought into a wine cellar, I were refreshed with the odor and cup of new wine. Typically by wine the grace of the Holy Spirit is noted; The wine cellar is the Church, in whose unity alone the Holy Spirit is wont to be given and received; which Church, gathered from the whole world, God built into one house for himself, which the Holy Spirit consecrated with his gifts. Which structure, because it stands on the foundation of greatest charity, he himself working, it is rightly added: He set in order charity in me. The charity of many is disordered, because what is first they put third, or fourth. First God is to be loved; second, parents; then children, afterward the household, who also, if good, are to be preferred to wicked children. According to this in the Gospel he places the proper at the love of anyone. You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole mind, and your neighbor as yourself, Mark 12. Enemies not with all strength, not as yourself, but simply: for it suffices that we love and do not hate. Or, he first loved me, and by loving gave that I might know how to love him. Or, he ordered, that is, with ordered charity, each of my members, that is all the elect, he joined to himself; he embraces the more eminent with greater affection. How far charity, when it has perfectly absorbed the mind, raises it above love of the weak, he shows when he adds:
2.5: 2.5 Stay me up. Now strengthened by the above, she so burns with the love of God that for excess of love or the pains inflicted languor of the flesh threatens. Or, stay me up, that is, you others, either more perfect or beginners, by working well be my refreshment, that I may rest in your good works, since I cannot yet rest in contemplating the face of God. Therefore stay me up, that you may have both present and future help, as I in my languor have. The more she kindles herself to love of the Bridegroom, the more she languishes from love of temporal things: whence she adds: I languish.
2.6: 2.6 His left hand. Seek not rest for your head elsewhere; for if you have his left hand, all things which are mine shall be given you. His left hand under my head. When the hearts of the faithful in this life are comforted by the participation in the sacraments, by the pledge of the Spirit, by the solaces of the Scriptures: which God also gives for the help of pilgrimage: the right hand will embrace, when after this life we shall receive heavenly rewards. The left, that is the present life, and the temporal gifts of God, while by hope it strengthens the mind, is under the head given for consolation: and the right, that is eternal life will embrace, as protecting, when through reward he will glorify us. As: The temporal benefits of God help me in this place of pilgrimage that I may rest a little from the desires and disturbances of the world, and the promise of eternal things delights the more.
2.7: 2.7 I adjure you. The primitive Church converted to the Gentiles, and as it were in their person speaking hitherto, when from inward love she now suffers failing of the body; the Bridegroom admonishes the new Church not to disturb her by sinning. How lovable to God is the repose of this Church and of any faithful soul is declared by the answer of the Bridegroom. By the roes. That is, if you wish to be comparable to roes or harts in the height of virtues and the more precious foods, and in the knowledge what medicine is fitting for your wounds, if you have wounds. Roes and harts, clean animals, enemies of poisons, ruminating, figure the works of spiritual virtues, against the snares of the venomous enemy. Harts at the time of love departing from their country, one with its head laid on the haunches of another sustains itself, going in order, the first carries, the last is only carried, the first being tired, the last takes its place, when dogs pursue through thickets with antlers laid on the back they escape unharmed. With dim eyes they eat the serpent, and having drunk of the fountain recover sight, and lay aside superfluities. So the saints by love of God renounce earthly things: bear one another's burdens, for the less burdened with sins lighten the burdened, by forgiving, by praying for them; the strength given through the Holy Spirit they put under their mind, while pressed by the wicked, and so pass unharmed; they eat the devil, that is, annihilate him in themselves, and having drunk of the fountain, that is Christ, recover inward sight, and put off the skin, that is, become free from sins. Stir not up. GREGORY. If subjects sin in anything, on account of which the teachers are forced to rise from rest, they not only incur the punishment of that sin, but are also punished for the disturbance of the teachers, because he who presumes to disturb teachers intent on heavenly things loses even the virtues he believed he had. To the oath of the Bridegroom, the bride gladly assents, and hearing this determination added, namely, till she herself will, perceives that it is secretly enjoined on her that she of her own accord wish to rise, she promises therefore that she will rise and proposes such a Bridegroom for whom she wills, and a fitting time. For after the apostles placed in the primitive Church of the Gentiles had brought themselves and others to such perfection as to be now free for contemplation, again she understands that the necessity has been laid on her of running through the whole world and building new Churches.
2.8: 2.8 The voice of my beloved. This is she whom I heard adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem not to rouse me: I rejoice hearing his consoling voice, though I do not yet see his face; yet with the mind lifted to heaven, I already taste some sweetness of future beatitude, even in this present. Leaping upon the mountains. He leaps on the mountains, and as it were sets his feet, by which sign it is known he was there, because he is imitated through passion and the conversation of life. He made a leap from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger onto the cross, from the cross into the sepulchre, from the sepulchre returned into heaven. He it is who was lifted above all mountains and hills, that is, the heights of the saints both greater and lesser. Skipping over the hills. On the hills no marks of feet appear, but they have received the shadow of one flying over: because even if not as those greater ones, yet to some degree they imitate and are visited by him. Mountains and hills are those who surpass the general conversation of the Church, like the flowery plain of the fields, by singular purity of mind, and departing from the lowest contemplate the heavenly more closely. On which he leaps, because he illumines the hearts of the lofty by frequent visitation; and he does not stay, but leaps and skips: because this sweetness of contemplation is brief and rare, on account of the heaviness of the flesh, because the earthly habitation weighs down the sense thinking many things.
2.9: 2.9 Like. Because he sees acutely, and dwells on the heights of the mountains, he leaps swiftly. Whence also he is more rarely seen by us: he always ascends from the nativity to the bosom of the Father. Like. And although by his divinity he so surpasses all, yet he was made man, for me born of the Gentile and the seed of the patriarchs. In the assumption of flesh and humanity he is compared to the roe; in the variety of virtues and miracles to the young hart. The hart by the breath of its nostrils draws the serpent out of caves, and the poison's destruction overcome, delights in the food. Since in these verses the sublimity of the contemplative life is expressed, it remains to show the perfection of the active life, which is common to the whole Church. Whence follows. Behold he stands, etc. Behind our wall. The wall which separates us from his sight is the condition of mortality, which we deserved by sinning, who were so made that if we did not sin, all the elect would behold the divine light untired: to behold which very few more perfect now, purified by faith, with labor attain: but in this wall the mercy of God made windows and lattices whence he made us look out, because to minds, though he pressed them down, he opened the grace of his knowledge, and looks upon us with frequent light of his inspiration. By the view of which inspiration, because this chiefly God does, to provoke us from temporal things to deserve the heavenly, it is rightly added: Behold my beloved speaks to me, who above admonished the daughters of Jerusalem to guard my rest: he sends me to cultivate the vineyards showing the opportunity. Behind the wall. Morally, if you have made your building, God will come behind your wall, looking through the windows, that is, he carefully beholds through the five senses; for where the Bridegroom does not look, death ascends: whence Jeremiah: Behold death has come up through our windows, Jeremiah 9; through the nets. All things are full of the nets of the devil, by which you would be caught, were it not that the Bridegroom subjected himself to the nets of the world who eminently, and tearing, made a way, that you may say: Our soul has been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers, Psalm 123. Through the windows. As the sun entering through windows illumines the house, so Christ by the example and admonition of the apostles has enlightened us. As through the lattices, that is, through small openings small light enters, so obscure knowledge through the prophets.
2.10: 2.10 Arise, make haste. That is, interrupt contemplation, and labor for the acquisition of others; or arise from love of earthly things. Arise, all things have their time; he who just now adjured the daughters of Jerusalem not to disturb the beloved: behold he invites her to labor. Arise, make haste. GREGORY. When she is now led out of the body of corruption, the rain is passed for her, because the torpor of the present life is gone, and she is led out to contemplate God in substance, nor are now the drops of words necessary, that the rain of preaching ought to be poured in. For what she could hear less she will see more. Then the flowers appear in the earth, when from the life of eternal beatitude the soul begins to taste certain first sweetnesses, which already she smells in flowers as she goes out, which after she has gone out, she will have more abundantly in fruit. The time of pruning is come. Our pruning then happens when we leave the fruitless and noxious corruption of the flesh, that we may come to the fruit of the soul, which fruit is most abundant to us. In pruning, indeed, barren branches are cut off, that those which are able may bear fruit more abundantly. Therefore arise, because I suffering for you stilled the waves. Come. To bestow also care of salvation on neighbors by zeal of diligent preaching, that you may deserve to be received with a great company to the wedding. As: you believe you will come, if you are free for contemplation: but you will come better through labor of this kind. You must preach, because since knowledge is already in you, there is also in those to whom I send you the opportunity of receiving.
2.11: 2.11 The rain is gone. I, rising from the dead, the tempest suppressed, restored tranquillity. Now it is easier to preach, since some are already converted, than before, when no one yet had believed.
2.12: 2.12 The flowers. As: Those who already believe and already work good, you can give as example to others: these you can propose to others as example, who already suffer the sickle cutting off vices. For your rest you ought not to give up preaching, because Christ, who was in great rest with the Father, in a way intermitted rest for preaching. The time of pruning. Now the useless branches of vain religion cut off, the hearts of men are prepared for the future fruit of faith, now vices also are cut off, because the time of remission of sins is come. The voice of the turtle is heard. The Holy Spirit, when he speaks of the more hidden sacraments, and what many do not take in, is signified by the name of turtle. Whence he appears also to Moses and to one: when of humble things which reach all, he is taken through the dove, whence also at the Jordan, many standing by, he appeared not in a turtle but in a dove. The voice of the turtle, the voice of the apostles, or of any preachers, who by their song announce the departure of winter and the coming of spring, who in place of song give humble groaning, who are lovers of chastity, who always dwell on the ridges of mountains, or on the tops of trees, and flee the conversation of men, while placed in the body in the world, they have their conversation in heaven, mindful of their sojourning and of the country promised them.
2.13: 2.13 The fig tree. He calls green figs the early and unripe, which are not fit for eating, which even if shaken, fall at a light touch: therefore the turtle sounding, that is the apostles preaching, the Synagogue put forth green figs, that is cast away the immature understanding of legal observance. Or thus: The Synagogue produced the apostles, who would minister sweet food to their believers. And because the Synagogue putting forth the apostles, the faith and salvation of the whole world followed, it is rightly added. The vines in flower. By the flowering the beginnings of the manifold Churches, from that which was first planted at Jerusalem, from whose flower the juice pressed makes a kind of cup, suited to health and pleasure, which gladdens the heart of man.
2.14: 2.14 In the clefts. In the wounds of Christ the Church sits and nests: when in the passion of the Lord she places the hope of her salvation, and by this trusts to be protected from the snares of the hawk, that is the devil, and in the same begets others. In the clefts. In faith, or in the capacity in which the faithful placed are safe from enemies. A wall is a heap of stones joined together without mortar, so the apostles are united by the same faith and the same sacraments. Show me. She did not yet have confidence to behold the glory of God with face unveiled; but because she is now adorned, it is said: Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears. The face is shown to the Lord by working rightly: the sound of voice is shown by preaching wholesomely. Be not ashamed to preach the cross of Christ, though it seem folly to unbelievers, which the apostles of Christ preached, who are the wall and fortification of the Church. Or, the walls are the prophets and patriarchs, in whom the apostles have refuge. What of beauty you have within, and have learned in the secret of quiet, show in public action for the profit of others: for to me who see the inmost, I reckon your face shown when I consider good action shown for the profit of neighbors. In my ears. Not strange ones, that is, to my love, not to any earthly thing, weigh both work and voice. For your voice. Not another's, but that which on the day of betrothal you promised to serve me.
2.15: 2.15 Catch us. Since it does not suffice us to set our life before others as example, and to make good preaching, unless we also correct the erring, and defend the weak from the snares of others, rightly it is said catch not for you, but for us; in this you serve me, in this I will reward you. Foxes are hidden in holes, and when they appear, never run in straight courses, so heretics. For our vineyard. Beautifully, when above vineyards in plural, here vineyard in singular, because many vineyards by faith and charity one: and therefore those are to be expelled who wish to rend it by heresies.
2.16: 2.16 My beloved to me. To such a speech of the beloved, soon the friend answers with the simplicity of a dove's heart, and promises to obey the enjoined office; as if she said, he not only exhorts, but also helps. My beloved to me. He is joined to me by sincere love, and I to him. Or, my beloved makes me such an exhortation, and I show him face and voice. Or, my beloved to me, not to another, namely, he will give grace and repay fruit; and I to him, not to any other, not in another crowd of men, but by entire obedience and devotion shall I be glued fast. To all these senses aptly fits what follows: Who feeds among the lilies. He is fed in us, because we are his body and members of the Member; he himself feeds us, who is the head. He feeds among the lilies, when the faithful, who are his members, are perfected by the examples of the faithful before them in love of the heavenly. Lilies. They are wont to heal burned limbs: so the saints, if perchance they see the hearts of neighbors burned with the flame of vices, apply the refreshment of consolation and exhortation. Because this feeding of the Lord, which is done in the progress of his saints, reaches to the end of the world. For when they come to the vision, in which they will not profit further, it is rightly added: Till the day break.
2.17: 2.17 Return, be like. Set your steps on the lofty minds, and from them sometimes by condescending appear to the lower who are in the valley. Return, be like. And because you provoke to establishing and cultivating Churches, and to driving away the wiles of the foxes, and that I should show you my face, though your face I do not yet see clearly, and by myself I am not sufficient, I beseech, illumine my heart more perfectly and the hearts of those to whom I am to preach.
3.1: 3.1 In my bed. The preachers from Judea praying, behold the Gentile world, breathed upon by the divine Spirit, comes to the knowledge of its salvation, and holds the found one with firm love. Whence follows: The voice of him fully entering. In my bed. GREGORY. Morally the holy soul makes for itself a bed in the night, while fleeing all the disturbances of the world, it prepares a secret place in which to rest. In this bed it seeks the beloved: because while free from anxieties, it rests in seeking how it may come to him: but while it lives in the world, it does not perfectly shake off the darkness of the world, and the more heavily it suffers, the more frequently it seeks, and more fervently him, whom found it will no more suffer darkness. But because in this world it does not find, therefore it is added: I sought him, and found him not. Because it burns with the greatest desire, and whatever it holds does not suffice it, until it find the Delight, therefore it adds the perseverance of the search, I will rise, and will go about the city. In my bed. Since Adam sinned, man began to rest in earthly things, and yet, reason leading, as through a dream understanding true beatitude, he thought it consisted in earthly things. JEROME. Morally. In the bed the soul seeks God, when in its leisure indeed it desires to see God, and desires to go out to him from the prison of the flesh, but it is not granted: and the Bridegroom hides himself, that not found he may be sought the more ardently. And I found him not. GREGORY. Because to me the Gentile world neither angel, nor prophet, nor any teacher in doubts showed the light of divine knowledge, therefore I found not, which when I discovered that it could not be found in bed, I purposed in my mind to rise from the bed of carnal pleasures, and to gird myself to the labor of saving search, and by land and sea publicly and privately to go to the schools of all whom I should hear to be wise. The streets are the spiritual men, who while they go toward heavenly things keep the narrow way. The squares, that is, the secular, who follow many pleasures, and go on the high way. She goes about all therefore, because she beholds in mind and imitates all the saints who are or were: even in the secular she sometimes finds what avails for the search of the Bridegroom: but after showing the doubled labor of the search, she again adds the difficulty of finding: I sought, and found not: but while she seeks and does not find, she herself both is sought and is found: Whence it is said: The watchmen found me. I sought. After wandering the world with very great labor, the words of the wise discussed, I could learn nothing certain about the way of truth.
3.3: 3.3 The watchmen found me. When I inquired thus, the Lord seeing this earnestness of inquiry, at length deigned to manifest himself and to her to whom he had inspired to seek he gave to find. Have you seen him whom my soul loves? GREGORY. To those wishing to teach, this one burning with excessive love first addresses, Have you seen him whom she loves. The Church questions the watchmen, when she intently receives preaching, and bears fruit in the showing forth of good works in it.
3.4: 3.4 When I had a little passed by them. THE SAME. She passes them, because in them she sees the form of him whom she seeks; and yet she passes, because she begins to imitate and behold God, who is beyond. Peter passes the watchmen, while he despises the prophets, and says to the Lord of the prophets: You are Christ, the Son of the living God, Matthew 16. Till I bring him in, etc. Until at the end of the world I shall strive to recall to his faith the Synagogue, through which I received hearing by faith, and the mystery of regeneration. The Gentile Church at the end will recall the Synagogue, which had first called her through the apostles.
3.5: 3.5 I adjure you. Christ hearing that he is to be led in by these, adjures them not to put an impediment to him. I adjure you. Therefore this verse is repeated in the canticle of love, to designate that the Lord has no less care of the Church from the Gentiles than of that gathered from the Jews: but bears an equal solicitude for the peace of both. For this queen of the south is captured by love of the Bridegroom no less than the first friend from the Jews. And the harts. It is of the hart in old age to eat the serpent, and for thirst conceived from the poison to hasten to the fountain, and by drinking thence to grow young, its hair and horns falling: which befits each faithful person through the washing of baptism.
3.6: 3.6 Who is she. Further he treats of the Church converted from the Gentiles, how having received the foundation from the apostles, then through succession of times and promotions of degrees she has been multiplied. Who is this? The Jews converted, seeing the Gentiles also converted and equally received into love of the Bridegroom; not from envy, but as wondering, and rejoicing together in the fellowship of the brethren, inquire whether salvation is promised to the Gentiles: which had been much doubted. Who goes up. At the same time, and sleeps, when she alienates herself from carnal desires of the Church, and by good works draws near to the vision of her Creator. Through the desert. That is through the midst of the Gentiles, who were fruitful in no fruit of virtues, whom no prophet or angel had instituted for the worship of God, or: Through the desert like a pillar of smoke, because separated from the allurements of the world, she is given to heavenly precepts. Smoke at the same time partly rises, partly that which rose before is wont to vanish in the higher places: so the Church, in some of her members is ever newly begotten, in some who were born before she is ever gathered to the heavenly. Smoke born of fire ascending on high gradually withdraws itself from human sight: so the Church kindled with love of God by the fire of the Holy Spirit alone ceases not to ascend, until, withdrawn from earthly things, she is snatched to the invisible things of heaven. Of aromatics. Note that, recalling the aromatics, first she puts myrrh, then frankincense, and afterwards all the powders of the perfumer, because first it is to mortify the concupiscence of the flesh, afterwards to offer to God the appeasing vows of the heart, and so with humility to grow in every kind of virtue. Powders. Reduced to powder they avail for the making: so virtues, when they do not lift up the mind, but are reduced as to powder in the estimation of the doer, lead to perfection. The perfumer, either the man who gives effort to virtues: or God, who bestows virtues.
3.7: 3.7 Behold the bed. To the former friend wondering the Gentile world answers, determining whither she ascends, namely to the bed, and by what means she ascends, namely the midst is strewn with charity, and proves herself to have come into the same love of the Bridegroom, in which the former is: because she likewise has the wedding array, and has preachers whom God would not have sent to us unless he had foreordained them. Behold the bed. The bed of the true peacemaker, eternal beatitude, in which the king rests with the saints, to which the Church through the desert partly arrives daily, at last will arrive perfectly. Or even the bed of God is in the present the quiet conversation of the saints. Both beds the most valiant surround: because both the present quiet, and the peace of the Church the preachers guard against incursions, and the inward quiet of the heavenly country the more perfect behold with fixed intention. Israel. That is a man seeing God, by which name all are rightly called who tend to the joys of the divine vision. Among whom the most valiant are those who are either raised by the gift of heavenly contemplation, or undertake the ministry of preaching.
3.8: 3.8 All holding swords. Who unceasingly have the word of God ready, both to cut off superfluities in themselves and in subjects, and to repel and trample enemies. All holding swords. They hold the word of God, and are skilled how to use it, as much to expugn others as themselves as to vices. Most expert in war. Because for so many thousands of years they fought against the devil in the frailty of flesh, they are taught by continual use. Because of fears. Lest the snares of the tempter, if they find them secure and unarmed, strike them down: and lest, they being overthrown, the bed which they ought to have guarded be defiled, namely, lest the present peace of the Church be violated, and so the future beatitude be lost.
3.9: 3.9 A litter. Not only by this, that both in the present I rest in the bed of Solomon, and hasten to the future bed, and have the most valiant guards, does it appear that salvation is promised to the Gentiles: but also by this, that he made of us a kind of litter, that is that it carry from place to place the dispensers of his word, or those in whom he himself is carried through the world. Or thus: The Peacemaker, to whose bed I hasten, has so fortified me: and this he did through the litter, that is through the apostles, by whom, as in a chair, he is carried, whom he sent for my or our salvation.
3.10: 3.10 The reclining place of gold. That is, his watchers full of divine wisdom, or he makes a reclining place in the litter, when he promises to the faithful the hope of perpetual rest. Gold, because he prepares the rest of his vision shining with glory. The going up of purple. The steps are those by which anyone can climb first to the virtues, afterward to the holy of holies: which are purple, that is ready for martyrdom. Or, the virtues themselves are the steps, which are the true purple: with which faithful souls are adorned. Or, Christ himself the ascent, through whom one enters both the Church and heaven. Purple, because he washed us in his blood: and no one enters the Church unless imbued with the sacraments of the Lord's passion. The midst he covered with charity. Or with charity, with which he suffered for us. The midst, that is, the hearts of the Church, he prepared like a floor, where faithful souls may rest softly: because he filled it all within with love of the heavenly: whence he adds: For the daughters of Jerusalem. For the souls burning with desire for heavenly things because the more he loved us, the more he kindles us to suffer for him. The midst. GREGORY. Behold consolation. He who cannot shed blood for the Lord, let him love his neighbor for the daughters of Jerusalem, because they are not to be called sons, that is firm, but daughters, who through charity are not alien to the building of God.
3.11: 3.11 Go forth and see, etc. In beautiful order after recounting the gifts of the king, she begins to proclaim his very appearance and adornment, and invites to see him. And the order and succession of this Church is to be attended to, which instituted from the first-fruits of the Jews, admonishes that first Church, now tepid after the apostles, by prelates, judges, and other degrees, that the mother render a return to the successors and fellow-sufferers of those by whom she was preached. In the diadem. As hidden in the humanity by which he conquered the devil: and the flesh was the cause of this victory: unless God were overshadowed with flesh, the devil would not attack him. In the diadem, that is, in that crown of thorns with which his Judea crowned him. With which his mother crowned him. With which humanity his mother honored him: in that she is a virgin, not defiled like other women, with the filth of original sin: and she sends us to the history. As: Believe the nativity, passion, resurrection. This description is extended for the manifoldness of the Church. Of his betrothal. If we refer his to the mother, we say at the time of the annunciation: if to the faithful, of the resurrection, which was the chief joy, because then the human race was set free.
4.1: 4.1 How beautiful you are. Since the bride converted from the Gentiles is now of such perfection as in turn to preach to the Jews and praise the Bridegroom: she also receives a worthy recompense of praise from the Bridegroom. This description is extended for the manifoldness of the Church. Beautiful in action, because like a pillar of smoke she goes up through the desert, beautiful in preaching, because she draws her neighbors to her fellowship. Eyes. That is, your senses by contemplation of spiritual things are excellent and reverend. By parts he intends to praise. Besides. Great is the glory of the open work, but far incomparably eternal reward, which cannot be seen. Your hair. That we may the more easily make everything clear, let us run briefly through each. Hairs are the voluntary poor. The cheeks, the highest prelates. The teeth of the cheeks, others inferior prelates. The lips, the preachers. Your hair. If in the eyes is taken the keenness of spiritual senses, in the hair can be marked the plurality of thoughts, which all tend to one end of heavenly good. Whence they are likened to goats, which are clean animals, and seek the steeps of rocks for pasture. Which came up. He puts one of the natures of the goat, that so it may be understood of others, and that virtue he preaches more which he perceives the hearers need more. Which came up. Of him who is a testimony to those imitating him, as he himself promised: He that shall confess me before men, etc., Luke 12.
4.2: 4.2 Your teeth as flocks of sheep that are shorn. As in the hair the frailer people of the Church, who supply numerousness, are signified: so in the teeth the stronger, apt to rule the Church, who prevail by firmness. From the washing, all. It is for all to be purified by baptism: it is for the perfect, and chiefly those to whom the care of sheep is committed, to renounce all that they possess. With twin lambs. That is with like offspring, because they make others such as they are themselves. Or, double offspring, the works of twin charity, as the faithful converted from both peoples. Or, faith and work. And none barren. Nor are they reckoned among the barren who, washed, are at once snatched from this life. For they have had the offspring of faith which they confessed either for themselves, or others for them. They have had also the vow of good working, which among the sheep of Christ, if they had been waited for, they would have exercised in fellowship, whence it is said: Being made perfect in a short space, he fulfilled a long time, Wisdom 4.
4.3: 4.3 Like a scarlet lace. Preachers are called a lace, because they restrain flowing thoughts in the hearts of men by their preaching, lest they flow away and press down the eyes of the heart. Scarlet. Because they cease not to preach the price of the Lord's blood by which the Church was redeemed: or because holy preaching is aflame with the ardor of charity. Your lips. The teeth that grind: the lips that open what is ground. Your speech sweet. While they do what they say, they set their preachings before men as savory foods. As a piece of a pomegranate, so your cheeks. In the color red without, the will for martyrdom: in the white grains which are seen when the rind is broken, the whiteness of virtues: which is increased while the flesh is crushed: whiteness also when, the passion fulfilled, they shine with miracles. In the cheeks modesty, in the pomegranate the passion of Christ. The Church therefore has a blush in the cheeks, when she confesses by words the sacrament of the Lord's passion, and shows whiteness when, beaten by pressures, she proves the chastity of a pure heart, and by deeds lays open what grace of salvation the cross has. Without that which is hid. Though what appears outwardly is great: yet greater things they retain in secret, which the divine eyes alone see. It lies hid. The confession of the life-giving cross all in the Church can hear, they can see the pressures of the Church, or even the miracles divinely conferred on the Church herself, unbelievers with believers can behold: but the soul alone knows with how great love of the invisible life she is held, with how great love toward God and neighbor she is aflame.
4.4: 4.4 Like the tower of David. The tower is the impregnable constancy of preachers, which for defending the buildings of faith, and for repelling the darts of enemies, is built by the strong hand of God, and desirable king, with bulwarks: that is, with knowledge of the divine Scriptures, when he opens the sense, that they may understand the Scriptures, and by the sayings of predecessors confirm their preaching, bulwarks also, the gifts of miracles, by which preaching is built up. For bodily diseases healed, one more easily comes to the salvation of the soul. Your neck. We stretch the neck when we look farther: so preachers, the neck, for watching enemies from afar: Tower, for strength and for the lofty contemplation of heavenly joys. Or, neck, because they send foods down into the body, or because they join the body to the head: whence, The Lord gives bread, and the disciples set it before the crowds. For one reason preachers are called eyes; for another, teeth: for another, cheeks: for another neck. The bulwarks are in the divine Scriptures the unbreakable sentences, in which they are safe who from afar defend themselves against assailants. A thousand shields. The shield is this most firm reason, relying on which they voluntarily go forth against heretics, and fortify themselves while they strike them. All armor. That is, every instruction, either of working or heavenly doctrine, by which the saints not only escape, but also overcome the battle lines of the malignant: while they draw some back from error or vices: all of which depend on the prelates, because from them we receive the example of resisting and conquering.
4.5: 4.5 Two breasts. By many figures the same mysteries of the Church are repeated; but repeated they always bring something new, and by the very novelty more delight the minds of hearers. Two breasts therefore, the preachers from the two peoples, who are called eyes because they advance hidden things. Teeth, because they correct the wicked, and carry them over into the body of the Church: Neck, because they minister the vital breath, preaching eternal joys, and the foods of doctrine. Breasts, because they pour milk upon the little ones in Christ, who are the fawns of the roe, because acutely they discern what is to be done, and fly from the valley of tears with the swift course of working. Twin, because they preach the same faith, the same sacraments: who lest the milk they supply fail in them are fed with the flowers of the Scriptures and the examples of the saints by always recollecting them. Two fawns. Two peoples, who through humility understand themselves little and sinners, but running with charity, pass over all obstacles of the world, and by leaps of contemplation ascend to the heights. Who feed. Because in these they have refreshment who flower with virtues and shine, while they cannot yet see from near the very God whom they desire.
4.6: 4.6 Till the day break. After there will be neither time of teaching nor of learning, but all the darkness of this world being consummated, all will shine as the sun. I will go to the mountain. And because the Church is such in each. I will go, that is, I will add grace, to the lower as well as the greater. I will go. Because I shall gather new peoples daily. And since the discourse is to the Church of the Gentiles, the calling of the Synagogue which is to be at the end of the world, can not unfittingly be seen promised: or the calling of any nations whatever. Whence soon concerning the most ample beauty of one and the same Church, which is to be gathered either from the Jews or from any nations throughout the whole world, it is added, You are all fair.
4.7: 4.7 You are all fair. Not only in the choicer members which I have enumerated, but also in those who seem little and frail.
4.8: 4.8 Come from Libanus. GREGORY. And because I go to you, you ought to come to me, in thought, speech, work. Or, the first step is in the flesh for good work: the second in the absolution of the flesh to receive beatitude in the soul: the third, the body received, when in the resurrection they receive double robes. Come by faith, come by work, come leading others: or come three times for the faith of the Trinity. Libanus a mountain of Phoenicia, in Hebrew is interpreted whitening, in Greek frankincense: whence above, I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense. While the preachers convert such to salvation, the crown grows from princes conquered by their struggle. Come. As: fear not, lest you come alone: because I will add many to you. From the top of Amana. Amana is a mountain of Cilicia, Sanir and Hermon mountains of Judea, in which lions dwell, by whom demons are marked, who rage against us: and because those are converted whose hearts were dens of lions, while in turn the Lord is believed by their confession, they are as it were crowned from the lions' dens, from which the lion is driven. By Amana we have those whom he himself, and through whom others the devil deceives and crushes by the vigilance of great zeal. By Sanir, those to whom ignorance of such deception flies. By Hermon, such as are as it were by nature prompt to wickedness, not that the devil designates. By the den of lions, those to whom, and through whom the savagery of persecution rules over others. By leopards, heretics, whom by distinct wiles he deceives, from the principal ones of each of whom God confers the crown of victory on his own. From the dens of lions. Lions, for pride, or violence. Leopards for cruelty or variation of malignant arts. By the name of mountains the proud hearts of unbelievers are designated.
